## Summary

**Task.** Assign each contract provision in LEDGAR (LexGLUE; 80,000 provisions
from SEC filings) to one of 100 provision types.

**Final model.** TF-IDF over word 1-2-grams plus a down-weighted block of
n-grams from the first 20 words of the provision, fed to a one-vs-rest linear
SVM with C = 1, trained on the cleaned train + validation splits.

**Held-out test performance** (10,000 provisions, scored only after the model was frozen):

| Metric | Estimate | 95% bootstrap interval |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy (= micro-F1) | `r pct(acc$estimate)` | `r pct(acc$lower)` – `r pct(acc$upper)` |
| Macro-F1 | `r pct(f1$estimate)` | `r pct(f1$lower)` – `r pct(f1$upper)` |
| Top-3 accuracy | `r pct(topk$accuracy[topk$k == 3])` | |

The published LexGLUE models are trained on the training split only. The same
pipeline fitted that way scores `r pct(bench$accuracy[6])` accuracy and
`r pct(bench$macro_f1[6])` macro-F1 on test, against 87.2 / 82.4 for LexGLUE's
TF-IDF + SVM baseline and 88.6 / 83.6 for its best transformer
(RoBERTa-large). A carefully tuned sparse linear model is therefore on par
with the published transformer results on this task; differences of a few
tenths of a point are inside the bootstrap interval.

**Against a fine-tuned transformer.** Legal-BERT-small, fine-tuned on the
same training split within a CPU-only budget (`r tf_sum$epochs` epochs,
`r round(tf_sum$train_minutes / 60, 1)` h), reaches
`r pct(tf_acc("Legal-BERT-small (fine-tuned)"))` accuracy and
`r pct(tf_head$estimate[4])` macro-F1 on test — `r pp(tf_diff$difference[1])`
and `r pp(tf_diff$difference[2])` relative to the SVM trained on the same
split (section 7). It had not converged, so this understates what a
transformer can do with more compute.

**Why the number can be trusted.**

* *Target shuffling.* With labels permuted, the complete cross-validated
  pipeline scores `r pct(shuf$null_mean[shuf$metric == "accuracy"])` accuracy on
  average (maximum over `r shuf$n_perm[1]` permutations:
  `r pct(shuf$null_max[shuf$metric == "accuracy"])`) against
  `r pct(shuf$observed[shuf$metric == "accuracy"])` with the real labels on the
  same sample: the pipeline cannot manufacture signal.
* *Resampling.* 5-fold stratified CV, repeated with three fold assignments:
  fold-to-fold SD `r pts(rep_cv$sd_between_folds[1])`, repeat-to-repeat SD
  `r pts(rep_cv$sd_between_repeats[1])`.
* *Two untouched hold-outs.* Model families rank the same way on the validation
  split as in CV, and the test split was scored exactly once.

**What limits it.**

* The largest single sources of error are near-synonymous labels (Applicable
  Laws vs Governing Laws, Definitions vs Defined Terms, …): the 20 most
  confused pairs account for `r pct(sum(head(cpairs$n, 20)) / sum(cpairs$n), 0)`
  of all test errors, and they are a property of the label scheme.
* Performance depends on how familiar a provision looks. Test provisions with
  a near-twin in the training data (cosine ≥ 0.95) are classified with
  `r pct(last(bysim$accuracy))` accuracy; those with no close neighbour
  (cosine < 0.4) with about
  `r pct(weighted.mean(bysim$accuracy[1:2], bysim$n[1:2]))`.
* The official splits are chronological and their label mix drifts. The same
  train-only model scores `r pct(drift$accuracy[1])` in random-fold CV,
  `r pct(drift$accuracy[2])` on validation and `r pct(drift$accuracy[3])` on
  test, so there is no sign of degradation on later filings — but that is an
  observation about the two periods this corpus covers, not a guarantee.

## 1. Data

LEDGAR (Tuggener et al., 2020) as packaged in LexGLUE (Chalkidis et al., 2022):
`r format(60000 + 10000 + 10000, big.mark = ",")` provisions in three official
splits (60,000 / 10,000 / 10,000), one label out of 100 per provision.
`analysis/01_acquire.R` downloads the parquet files and records checksums.

### Labels

```{r}
fig("02_label_counts")
```

Class sizes range from `r imb$smallest` to `r format(imb$largest, big.mark = ",")`
training examples (`r round(imb$ratio)`×); the effective number of classes is
`r round(imb$effective_classes)`. Always predicting the largest class would be
right `r pct(imb$majority_baseline)` of the time. Accuracy alone would hide
failures on small classes, so macro-F1 is reported throughout.

```{r}
fig("02_label_split_consistency")
```

The validation label mix is close to train, the test mix is not (χ² goodness
of fit p = `r format(signif(gof$p_value[gof$split == "test"], 2), scientific = TRUE)`).
LexGLUE splits LEDGAR by filing year, so this is drift over time. Whether it
costs accuracy on later filings is tested in section 6 (it does not,
measurably).

### Text

```{r, out.width = "70%"}
fig("03_length_distribution")
```

Provisions are short (median `r len[["median"]]` words, 99th percentile
`r round(len[["q99"]])`). Length varies systematically by class:

```{r}
fig("03_length_by_class")
```

```{r}
fig("03_text_artefacts")
```

Numbers, section enumerators and typographic characters are common and carry
no information about the provision type, which motivates digit masking and
character repair in the cleaning step.

### Duplicates and leakage

There are no exact duplicate texts anywhere in the corpus. After masking
digits, case and punctuation ("template" fingerprint), however:

```{r}
dup |> transmute(Check = check, Rows = n, Share = pct(share, 2)) |> knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
fig("03_nearest_neighbour_similarity")
```

About `r pct(nn$share_ge_0.95[3], 0)` of test provisions have a near-identical
twin (cosine ≥ 0.95) in train. The same is true *within* train, so this is a
property of contract boilerplate rather than a flaw in the split, but it means
part of any score reflects recall of boilerplate (quantified in section 6).

### Class separability

```{r}
fig("04_umap_families")
```

```{r, out.width = "80%"}
fig("04_confusable_pairs")
```

Boilerplate classes form isolated islands. The pairs with the most similar
centroids are near-synonyms in the label scheme itself (Applicable Laws /
Governing Laws, Defined Terms / Definitions, …). These set a ceiling that is a
property of the labels, not of the model.

## 2. Cleaning

`provisionr::clean_corpus()` applies the decisions above to the **training
split only** and logs each step:

```{r}
clog |> transmute(Step = step, `Rows removed` = rows_removed, `Rows left` = format(rows_left, big.mark = ",")) |> knitr::kable()
```

```{r, out.width = "75%"}
fig("05_cleaning_effects")
```

Held-out rows are never dropped. Whether de-duplication helps was treated as an
open question and tested on the validation split (section 4): accuracy
`r pct(dedup$accuracy[2], 2)` with cleaned training data versus
`r pct(dedup$accuracy[1], 2)` with raw, i.e. no measurable difference — the
step is kept because it removes label noise and makes fold assignment honest,
not because it buys accuracy.

## 3. Features

All features are learned inside each training fold by `fit_featurizer()` and
applied with `bake_features()`. Candidate blocks: word n-gram TF-IDF, character
n-gram TF-IDF, a "head" block (n-grams of the opening words only) and twelve
dense surface statistics.

```{r}
fig("06_surface_statistics")
```

```{r, out.width = "75%"}
fig("06_head_purity")
```

Each block shows class signal in isolation. Whether it *adds* signal on top of
word n-grams is a different question, answered by ablation.

### Ablation, round 1

```{r}
fig("08_ablation_screening")
```

One change at a time against word 1-2-gram TF-IDF (linear SVM, C = 1, 20k
subsample, fold-wise paired differences). Sub-linear tf, idf and bigrams
matter; everything else is within noise, and the head block appeared to hurt.

### Ablation, round 2: a confound

Adding a unit-norm block rescales every document vector, which for an SVM acts
like changing C. Repeating the comparison across C and block weights reverses
the verdict on the head block:

```{r, out.width = "80%"}
fig("08_ablation_weights")
```

### Confirmation on the full training split

```{r}
conf |> transmute(`Feature set` = variant, Features = format(round(n_features), big.mark = ","),
                  `CV accuracy` = sprintf("%s ± %s", pct(accuracy_mean, 2), pct(accuracy_se, 2)),
                  `CV macro-F1` = sprintf("%s ± %s", pct(macro_f1_mean, 2), pct(macro_f1_se, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Selected: word 1-2-grams + head block (first 20 words, weight 0.5). Character
n-grams were dropped on cost (4× compute for a gain within noise); surface
statistics add nothing once n-grams are present.

### Baselines

```{r}
fig("07_baselines")
```

### Tuning

`r nrow(tuned)` configurations from `r n_distinct(tuned$family)` families, same
features and folds for all:

```{r}
fig("09_regularisation_paths")
```

```{r}
fig("09_best_per_family")
```

```{r}
best_fam |> arrange(desc(accuracy_mean)) |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `CV accuracy` = sprintf("%s ± %s", pct(accuracy_mean, 2), pct(accuracy_se, 2)),
            `CV macro-F1` = sprintf("%s ± %s", pct(macro_f1_mean, 2), pct(macro_f1_se, 2)),
            `Fit time (s)` = round(fit_seconds, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Selection and hold-out check

The CV winner is **`r winner`**. Before touching the test split, the best
configuration of every family was fitted on the full training split and scored
on the validation split, which had not been used for anything so far:

```{r}
fig("10_cv_vs_validation")
```

The ranking carries over (Spearman ρ =
`r round(cor(cvval$cv_accuracy, cvval$valid_accuracy, method = "spearman"), 2)`).
Validation scores are, if anything, slightly higher than the CV estimates; the
hold-out models were trained on all of the training split rather than four
fifths of it. The four tuned linear models are indistinguishable on validation
as well, so the choice among them is not consequential.

Two side questions were settled on the same hold-out:

```{r}
res("10_nonlinear_check") |>
  transmute(Model = model, `Validation accuracy` = pct(accuracy), `Validation macro-F1` = pct(macro_f1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Gradient-boosted trees beat a linear model on the same 100 LSA components, but
both are far behind the linear model on the full sparse representation: what
matters is keeping the n-gram detail, not adding non-linearity.

The selected configuration was then refitted on train + validation.

## 6. Robustness

### Boilerplate

```{r}
fig("13_accuracy_by_similarity")
```

```{r}
fig("12_slices")
```

```{r}
grp |> transmute(Scheme = scheme, `CV accuracy` = sprintf("%s ± %s", pct(accuracy_mean, 2), pct(accuracy_se, 2)),
                 `CV macro-F1` = sprintf("%s ± %s", pct(macro_f1_mean, 2), pct(macro_f1_se, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Keeping template twins in the same fold lowers the CV estimate by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (grp$accuracy_mean[1] - grp$accuracy_mean[2]))` pp: exact
boilerplate repeats inflate a naive CV a little, which is one reason the
training split was de-duplicated before any resampling. Similarity to the
training data matters far more broadly, as the first figure shows: accuracy
rises from `r pct(bysim$accuracy[1], 0)` for provisions unlike anything in
train to `r pct(last(bysim$accuracy), 0)` for near-twins.

### Temporal drift

```{r}
fig("13_temporal_drift")
```

The label mix of the test split differs significantly from train (section 1),
yet the train-only model does no worse on the later splits than random-fold CV
predicted: `r pct(drift$accuracy[1])` (CV) → `r pct(drift$accuracy[2])`
(validation) → `r pct(drift$accuracy[3])` (test). Re-weighting the test rows to
the training label mix changes test accuracy by only
`r pp(drift$accuracy[4] - drift$accuracy[3], 1)`. Two caveats: CV models are
trained on four fifths of the data, which by the learning curve below costs
roughly half a point, and each hold-out number carries about ±0.6 pp of
sampling error (2 SE). Within that resolution there is no sign that the model
degrades on newer filings — over the two periods this corpus covers.

### Learning curve

```{r}
fig("13_learning_curve")
```

### Resampling noise

```{r}
rep_cv |> transmute(Metric = metric, Mean = pct(mean, 2), `SD between folds` = pts(sd_between_folds),
                    `SD between repeats` = pts(sd_between_repeats)) |> knitr::kable()
```

## 7. Comparison with a fine-tuned transformer

To see what a pretrained language model adds, an open-source legal-domain
encoder was fine-tuned on the same data: **Legal-BERT-small**
(`nlpaueb/legal-bert-small-uncased`, `r format(round(tf_sum$parameters / 1e6), nsmall = 0)`M
parameters, CC-BY-SA-4.0). The protocol mirrors the SVM study — weights
trained on the train split only, epoch and hyper-parameters chosen on
validation, the test split scored once at the end — so the like-for-like
counterpart is the SVM fitted on the train split only.

**Compute constraint.** The environment has 4 CPU cores and no GPU. That
dictated the model (Legal-BERT-base would have needed about 2.6 hours per
epoch) and the budget: `r tf_sum$epochs` epochs at `r tf_sum$max_length` word
pieces, `r round(tf_sum$train_minutes / 60, 1)` hours of training. Learning
rate and input length were chosen in five small pilot runs
(`results/14_pilot_runs.csv`). Published LEDGAR results for transformers use
larger models and up to 20 epochs on GPUs, so this is a comparison at equal
*data*, not at equal *effort*.

```{r}
fig("14_training_curve")
```

Validation accuracy was still rising at the last epoch
(`r paste(pct(tf_hist$val_accuracy), collapse = " → ")`), so the transformer
had not converged within this budget; more epochs would probably narrow the
gap reported below, though the per-epoch gain was already shrinking.

### Headline

```{r}
fig("14_headline")
```

```{r}
tf_head |>
  mutate(value = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", pct(estimate), pct(lower), pct(upper)),
         metric = recode(metric, accuracy = "Accuracy (micro-F1)", macro_f1 = "Macro-F1")) |>
  select(Model = model, metric, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

On accuracy the transformer is `r pp(tf_diff$difference[tf_diff$metric == "accuracy"], 2)`
relative to the SVM (95% paired-bootstrap interval
`r pp(tf_diff$lower[tf_diff$metric == "accuracy"], 2)` to
`r pp(tf_diff$upper[tf_diff$metric == "accuracy"], 2)`; exact McNemar
p = `r format(signif(tf_mcn$p_value, 2), scientific = TRUE)`), and on macro-F1
`r pp(tf_diff$difference[tf_diff$metric == "macro_f1"], 2)`
(`r pp(tf_diff$lower[tf_diff$metric == "macro_f1"], 2)` to
`r pp(tf_diff$upper[tf_diff$metric == "macro_f1"], 2)`).

```{r}
tf_agree |> transmute(Outcome = outcome, `Test provisions` = format(n, big.mark = ","), Share = pct(share)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The SVM is the better model here, clearly so on macro-F1: the fine-tuned
network is weaker on small and confusable classes.

### Where they differ

```{r, out.width = "75%"}
fig("14_per_class")
```

The SVM has the higher F1 on `r sum(tf_pc$diff < 0)` of `r nrow(tf_pc)` classes,
the transformer on `r sum(tf_pc$diff > 0)`. Both find the same classes hard
(correlation of per-class F1 `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(tf_pc$f1_svm, tf_pc$f1_bert))`),
but the transformer collapses on some rare or near-synonymous ones — it never
correctly predicts *Applicable Laws* or *Assigns*.

```{r}
fig("14_slices")
```

The gap is not uniform. On provisions unlike anything in the training data
(similarity below 0.4) the two models are tied
(`r pct(tf_sl$bert[tf_sl$slice == "< 0.4"])` vs `r pct(tf_sl$svm[tf_sl$slice == "< 0.4"])`).
The SVM's lead comes from familiar boilerplate, where exact n-gram matches are
decisive, and from the longest provisions, which the transformer only reads up
to `r tf_sum$max_length` word pieces
(`r pct(tf_sum$share_truncated, 0)` of provisions are truncated).

### Do they complement each other?

```{r}
fig("14_ensemble")
```

Only a little. A weighted average of the two models' probabilities
(temperatures and weight fitted on validation) improves on the SVM by
`r pp(tf_ens_diff$difference[1], 2)` accuracy (95% interval
`r pp(tf_ens_diff$lower[1], 2)` to `r pp(tf_ens_diff$upper[1], 2)`), with no
reliable change in macro-F1. At least one of the two models is right on
`r pct(tf_ens$estimate[tf_ens$model == "Oracle (either model correct)"])` of
test provisions, so their errors overlap heavily.

```{r}
fig("14_confidence")
```

The transformer's temperature-scaled probabilities are better calibrated
(expected calibration error `r pct(tf_ece$ece[2])` vs `r pct(tf_ece$ece[1])`
for the SVM's soft-maxed margins). For deciding which predictions to trust,
the SVM's confidence ranking is at least as good.

### Cost

```{r}
tf_cost |>
  transmute(Model = model, Parameters = format(parameters, big.mark = ","),
            `Training time` = sprintf("%.1f min", train_minutes),
            `Time to score 10,000 provisions` = sprintf("%.0f s", test_predict_seconds),
            Hardware = hardware) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

(The SVM training time is the measured cross-validation fit time scaled to
the full training split.)

**Takeaway.** With the data and hardware available here, the sparse linear
model is more accurate, about `r round(tf_cost$train_minutes[2] / tf_cost$train_minutes[1])`
times cheaper to train and about `r round(tf_cost$test_predict_seconds[2] / tf_cost$test_predict_seconds[1])`
times faster to apply. That is not a general verdict on transformers for
this task: larger published models trained for longer on GPUs reach
88.2–88.6% accuracy, level with the SVM. Taken together, the evidence
suggests that on LEDGAR a pretrained encoder needs far more compute to match
a well-tuned bag of n-grams, and does not clearly beat it even then.

## 8. Limitations

* Test accuracy describes filings from the period right after the training
  data. Performance on later or structurally different contracts will be lower
  and should be monitored.
* Selecting one of `r nrow(tuned)` configurations by CV biases the CV estimate
  of the winner upward slightly; the validation and test scores are free of
  that bias, which is why they are the numbers to quote.
* The bootstrap interval reflects test-set sampling only, not the variability
  of retraining.
* The comparison with published results is indicative only: those are
  different training runs without reported intervals, and the final model here
  also uses the validation split.
* Linear models over n-grams cannot use context outside the provision, and the
  hardest label pairs are near-synonyms. That published transformer models
  score about the same suggests label ambiguity, rather than model capacity,
  is the binding constraint on this benchmark.
* The margin is a ranking score, not a calibrated probability.

## Reproducing

```sh
cd ledgar
make setup   # R packages + provisionr
make all     # steps 01-13 and this report
```

The process itself is tracked as tickets on an epiq board (snapshot in
`docs/epiq/board.md`); every commit subject starts with its ticket ref.
